Abdicate

AB-dih-kayt -- from Latin abdicare ('to disown, renounce'), ab- ('away, off') + dicare ('to proclaim, declare'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To abdicate is to formally give up a position of power or high office, or to abandon a duty or responsibility one is bound to carry out.

Weary after forty years on the bench, the judge chose to abdicate her seat rather than face a contentious re-election campaign.

Worked Example

Rather than face a messy public vote of no confidence, the club's longtime president decided to abdicate his position quietly at the end of the season.

That deliberate, formal act of stepping away from power or duty -- choosing to let it go rather than being forced out -- is exactly what it means to abdicate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

resign: To resign is to formally quit a job or position of your own accord — an everyday word for stepping down from any post. To abdicate is heavier and more formal: it is reserved for thrones, high offices, or a solemn duty someone walks away from entirely.

cede: To cede is to surrender something to someone else — territory, power, control — with the stress on handing it over to the other party. To abdicate stresses the act of stepping down itself: a ruler can abdicate without ceding power to anyone in particular.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

assume: to take on a role, duty, or responsibility

retain: to continue to hold or keep something

Where it sits · how complete the giving up is — relinquish → abdicate → renounce

relinquish vs. abdicate: Relinquish is milder than abdicate: a vice president may relinquish one board seat after a merger, while to abdicate is to give up a throne or duty entirely — a heavier, more absolute surrender.

renounce vs. abdicate: Renounce goes further than abdicate: a monarch who abdicates steps down from the throne, but an heir who renounces every future claim rejects it more absolutely, cutting the tie forever.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ab-

prefix — ab-: away, off (Latin)

root — dic-

root — dic-: to proclaim, declare (Latin (dicare))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ab- ('away') plus dicare ('to proclaim') plus the verb suffix -ate. To abdicate is to formally declare yourself away from a position -- publicly announcing that you are stepping down.

Use the root in a new word: dedicate

Use the root in a new word: dedicate: She decided to dedicate every weekend that summer to training for the marathon.

Word Choice

Abdicate is most often used for thrones and formal offices, but it also works for any serious duty someone deliberately walks away from, such as a parent who abdicates responsibility for a child.
